incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act (Alberta), R.S.A. 2000, c. B-9, ss. 6–20 (Incorporation), s. 13 (Name), s. 9 (Share Capital); Unlimited Liability Company Regulation, Alta. Reg. 226/2004
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta (Ministry of Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction)
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of Incorporation under Form 1 of the Business Corporations Act (Alberta)
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital for Alberta ULC; capital may be nominal (e.g., $1 CAD). No escrow requirement or capital deposit obligation under Alberta corporate law.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED that the Articles of Incorporation registered with the Alberta Corporate Registry are adopted and the subscribers are issued their subscribed shares. RESOLVED that the registered office of the corporation is established at the address recorded in the Articles and such address and the registered agent are approved. RESOLVED that the following persons are appointed as directors: [Name], [Name], and [Name]. RESOLVED that the officers are appointed as follows: [Name] as President, [Name] as Secretary, and [Name] as Treasurer. RESOLVED that the corporation shall open banking accounts with [Institution] and the directors are authorized to execute all documents necessary to implement these resolutions.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry / authorized service provider (Corporate Access Connect)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: File a NUANS (Newly Upgraded Automated Name Search) request through an Alberta Registry Agent or online service. Provide up to three proposed corporate names. Ensure the name includes or omits 'Unlimited Liability Company' as required. Await issuance of a NUANS report to confirm no conflict.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If name is refused or similar conflicting name exists, respond by submitting a revised name request with distinguishing words or obtaining a consent letter from the existing named corporation.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Drafting and Filing Articles of Incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry (Corporate Access Connect / appointed Registry Agent)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare the Articles of Incorporation in accordance with the ABCA and ULC Regulation. Specify unlimited liability status, share structure (authorized and issued classes), categories of directors (one or more, resident Canadian or Alberta resident as required), registered office address, and any special provisions. Submit the filed articles with the statutory fee and the NUANS report.
required_dossiers: Consent to act as first directors (signed)
Registered office and first board address form
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If Registry issues a defect or inquiry, file a corrected Articles or provide clarification within 30 days. If outright rejection, submit an amended application with the required changes and re-pay only the applicable correction fee, if any.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Appointment of Registered Office and Registered Agent
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry / registered office filing
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Identify an Alberta physical address for registered office (cannot be a P.O. Box). Appoint a registered agent (law firm, corporate service provider, or individual in Alberta). File the initial registered office information with the Registry or include it in the Articles; retain proof of filing.
required_dossiers: Registered office and registered agent form
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registry flags an incorrect address or agent consent is defective, file an amendment or change of registered office/agent form within 14 days to cure.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Organization Meeting and First Board Resolutions
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Corporate internal records / board of directors
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene an organizational meeting of the first directors. Adopt the pro-forma first board resolution addressing share subscription, appointment of officers, adoption of by-laws, approval of share certificates, and opening of corporate bank accounts. Document meeting minutes and have the secretary sign the minutes.
required_dossiers: Consent to act as directors and officers
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a director or officer fails to consent, hold a special meeting to appoint replacement and obtain written waiver or limitation of liability, if applicable.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry / CRA (tax registration) / municipal authorities
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Register with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) for corporate income tax account, GST/HST (if gross revenue exceeds $30,000), and payroll (if employees). File the Alberta Corporate Registry 'Initial Return' within 60 days of incorporation. For the design subscription business, apply for a municipal business license in the city of operation (e.g., Calgary, Edmonton). Maintain a corporate minute book and securities register.
required_dossiers: Proof of corporate existence (Articles/Notice of Filing)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If CRA or municipal filings are queried due to missing information, provide the requested supporting documents within 21 days. If the Initial Return is filed late, apply for cancellation of any administrative penalty under the Corporate Registry statutes.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not applicable – service business; municipal licensing authority as applicable (e.g., City of Calgary Business Licensing / City of Edmonton Integrated Development).
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: General business license / home–business authorization (if applicable); no provincial industrial or manufacturing permit required.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt – office-based professional design service; no physical development, emissions, or discharge-generating activity.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: N/A – zero-discharge office operation. If future physical expansion occurs, compliance with the Alberta Environmental Protection and Enhancement Act and local municipal wastewater and waste management bylaws would then apply.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: No special civil defense certification required. Occupancy fire safety clearance is issued by municipal fire marshal under the Alberta Fire Code. Worksite compliance with Alberta Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) Code is mandatory for employees, including ergonomic assessment, emergency exits, and first-aid kit availability. No industrial structural load inspection applicable.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Federal: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC) — national tax administration for corporate income tax (T2 returns), GST/HST (Part IX of the Excise Tax Act), payroll, excise, and GST/HST refunds. Provincial (Alberta): Alberta Corporate Registry (Service Alberta / Alberta Registries) — provincial incorporation, corporate registry filings, and annual returns; Alberta Finance — Alberta levies no provincial retail sales tax, does not participate in the HST, but imposes its own corporate income tax administered federally by the CRA under a tax-collection agreement. Portals: CRA Business Registration Online (BRO) at canada.ca; CRA My Business Account (MyBA); GST/HST NETFILE; Alberta corporate registry portal at corporate-registry.servicealberta.ca (CORES e-filing system).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Step 1 — Incorporate the Alberta ULC: file articles of incorporation in the unlimited liability form under the Business Corporations Act (Alberta) (R.S.A. 2000, c. B-9) with the Alberta Corporate Registry; obtain the Alberta incorporation number and certificate of incorporation; no minimum capital requirement applies; 100% non-resident (including U.S.) shareholding is permitted; a registered office in Alberta must be maintained and an Alberta-resident representative may be required for service of process. Step 2 — Federal Business Number (BN): under the federal-provincial one-stop business registration system, Alberta transmits the incorporation data to the CRA, which automatically issues the 9-digit BN; the ULC activates the program accounts — RC for corporate income tax, RT for GST/HST, RP for payroll (only if employees are engaged); RM/RE customs accounts are inapplicable because digital design exports involve no physical goods. Alternative: file paper form RC1, Request for a Business Number, directly with the CRA. Step 3 — GST/HST registration: the RT account becomes effective from the later of the incorporation date and the date the ULC exceeds the C$30,000 small-supplier threshold; because the ULC will be a zero-rated exporter, voluntary registration is strongly recommended to recover input tax credits (ITCs) on Canadian design-software subscriptions, contractor fees, rent, and marketing costs. Step 4 — Non-resident owner identification: CRA collects director/shareholder identity and jurisdiction of residence for FATCA/CRS exchange; if the U.S. parent has elected check-the-box (Form 8832), the CRA nonetheless requires the ULC to file a T2 return as a taxable Canadian corporation and to identify the U.S. owners on the CRA return schedules. Timeline: BN and program accounts issued within 2 to 5 business days; GST/HST account is effective immediately upon registration. Ongoing compliance: T2 corporate income tax return is due 6 months after fiscal year-end; GST/HST returns are due monthly, quarterly, or annually depending on net tax revenue (quarterly is standard for a small zero-rated exporter); Alberta corporate tax is assessed through the T2 with no separate provincial corporate tax return.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Pass_Through_Eligible — hybrid entity classification: (i) Canadian domestic tax law treats the Alberta ULC as an entity-level taxpayer, namely a taxable Canadian corporation under Income Tax Act s. 89(1), subject to Canadian tax on worldwide income; the federal basic rate of 38% is reduced by the 10% provincial abatement and the 13% general rate reduction to a 15% federal rate, plus Alberta corporate income tax at 8%, producing a combined headline rate of 23% on active business income (11% combined on the first C$500,000 of active business income where the small business deduction is available). (ii) For U.S. federal tax purposes, the ULC is an eligible entity: solely by reason of its unlimited liability feature, U.S. shareholders may check the box under Treasury Regulation Section 301.7701-3 (and consistent with Rev. Rul. 78-318) to classify the ULC as a disregarded entity for a single 100% U.S. owner or as a partnership for multiple owners, thereby creating a U.S.-Canada hybrid entity. (iii) The CRA does not recognize the U.S. flow-through election; the ULC remains a corporation in Canada, and the U.S. shareholder claims foreign tax credits for the Canadian corporate income tax paid on the ULC's export-design income. Territorial scope: residence-based worldwide taxation, with no territorial exemption and no Alberta provincial tax distinction in the GST/HST system other than the absence of a provincial sales tax component.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: (1) U.S. check-the-box election (IRS Form 8832): available to the ULC solely because of its unlimited liability status; default U.S. classification for a wholly owned ULC is disregarded entity; partnership classification applies for multi-owner ULCs; the election is prospective and generally locked for 60 months. (2) Canadian law provides no check-the-box analog; the ULC cannot elect to be a partnership or disregarded entity for Canadian federal or Alberta income tax purposes. (3) GST/HST elections: an election under ETA s. 273 can make taxable supplies between the ULC and a closely related Canadian corporation nil-valued; an election under ETA s. 240 permits GST/HST group registration with related Canadian registrants; an election under ETA s. 156 can fix the time of consideration for related-party supplies. (4) Hybrid mismatch treatment: Canada has not enacted BEPS Action 2 dual-inclusion or non-deduction rules specific to ULCs; CRA may nonetheless challenge aggressive ULC structures under the general anti-avoidance rule (Income Tax Act s. 245) and under the Canada-U.S. Treaty (Article VII permanent-establishment attribution) where the check-the-box election creates double non-taxation; the U.S. parent remains exposed to GILTI/Subpart F inclusions on the Canadian branch income in the United States.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada); prudential regulation delegated to the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI); AML/CFT enforcement by the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC); monetary policy and payments settlement infrastructure operated by Payments Canada (Lynx, ACSS) and the Bank of Canada.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada maintains full current-account and capital-account convertibility of the Canadian dollar (CAD) under IMF Article VIII. The Currency Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. C-52) and the Bank of Canada Act impose no foreign-exchange controls; the Exchange Control Act was repealed in 1952 and no reinstatement legislation exists. Profit remittance hurdles: an Alberta ULC may pay dividends, interest, royalties, and management fees to non-resident shareholders without Bank of Canada or OSFI approval; the only imposts are Part XIII Income Tax Act (Canada) withholding taxes (default 25%, treaty-reduced to 10% for US portfolio dividends, 5% for qualifying 10% corporate shareholders actively engaged in trade under Canada-US Treaty Article X; interest generally 0% on arm's-length lending; royalties 10%). The CAD floats freely; there is no dual-rate regime, no surrender obligation, and no prior approval for conversion. Capital-account openness is subject only to Investment Canada Act review for control acquisitions above the applicable WTO-investor enterprise-value threshold (C$1.055 billion in 2024) and to national-security screening. The UI/UX design subscription business qualifies as an exportable 'Design-As-A-Service'; invoicing in USD, EUR, or CAD is unrestricted, and subscription revenues may be accumulated in foreign currency indefinitely. Statutory reporting to the CRA of worldwide income converted at the Bank of Canada annual rate is required, but no treasury approval or exchange licence is needed for any transaction.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canada imposes zero surrender or retention requirements on export proceeds. The ULC may retain 100% of gross subscription receipts in foreign currency in domestic or offshore accounts for an unlimited period; no mandatory conversion ratio or repatriation timeline applies. The only compliance obligations are informational: (i) the CRA income tax filing reports all revenue converted to CAD at the applicable annual average exchange rate; (ii) a T106 Related-Party Transaction return must be filed if the ULC transacts with a non-resident controlling shareholder (including a US parent of the ULC); and (iii) FINTRAC imposes no reporting on ordinary commercial subscription credits below the electronic-funds-transfer threshold, while inbound/outbound EFTs of CAD 10,000 or more are automatically reported by the financial institution, not by the ULC. For intercompany settlement of design subcontractor payments abroad, the ULC must retain supporting invoices, contracts, and the banking purpose codes for CRA transfer-pricing audits, but no statutory surrender or licensing mechanism exists.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: Medium for Wise (Wise Payments Canada Inc.) and Airwallex as supplementary payment-corridor rails; Low for Revolut, N26, and pure offshore digital EMIs as primary bank accounts. Legal constraints: under the Bank Act (Canada), deposit-taking is restricted to chartered banks and authorized credit unions; a foreign EMI cannot accept 'deposits' in Canada and may operate only as a Money Services Business (MSB) registered with FINTRAC, with a Canadian presence or agent, a risk/AML compliance program, and no ability to hold corporate funds as fiduciary deposits. Wise is a registered MSB in Canada and may hold funds under a limited-purpose custodial arrangement, making it suitable for low-balance disbursement corridors, but the ULC must maintain its primary treasury accounts at a Tier-1 Schedule I bank. Stripe Billing is a payment processor (not an EMI) and remains the sanctioned subscription collection rail; its Canadian Merchant of Record (Stripe Payments Canada, Ltd.) requires a Canadian bank settlement account. Offshore EEA EMIs cannot passport into Canada; therefore any non-Canadian EMI holding ULC operating funds is non-compliant and must be avoided as a primary account.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Remote opening is permitted for Canadian-resident directors and signing officers via video-call identity verification under FINTRAC's PCMLTFA requirements (recognized electronic KYC acceptable). A non-resident director who will act as an individual signatory (e.g., the US parent CEO) must generally verify identity in person at a designated Alberta branch (Calgary or Edmonton) or before a commissioned notary whose certification is acceptable to the bank; most Tier-1 banks additionally require initial account-activation video or telephone interview with the Treasurer. ULCs with a non-resident ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) will be asked for an Alberta head-office address, a registered Alberta agent for service, and an Alberta-resident manager able to produce source-of-funds documentation. Directors cannot be entirely absent there must be at least one accountable person accessible in Canada during onboarding; there is no statutory requirement for a physical board meeting in Alberta, but banks may condition onboarding on a virtual board resolution certified by corporate counsel.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: The ULC's unlimited-liability structure is a recognized US tax-planning vehicle (IRS Form 8832 check-the-box), which may be perceived as tax-avoidance architecture or shell risk by onboarding compliance.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide (i) Alberta Certificate of Status and Articles of Incorporation; (ii) the US parent/LLC's IRS Form 8832 election showing disregarded-entity or partnership status; (iii) a written explanation of the legitimate Canadian-US tax alignment (deferral of Canadian withholding through ULC dividend deductibility); (iv) complete register of directors and UBOs with passport copies; (v) the signed engagement letter and subscription agreements with at least two named enterprise clients proving substantive business purpose.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: All-foreign ownership with a single non-resident director controlling both the ULC and settlement accounts may trigger elevated 'management and control' red flags under Canadian beneficial-ownership rules.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Evidence of Canadian substance: (i) Alberta head-office lease and utility bill in the ULC name; (ii) appointment of an Alberta-registered agent for service; (iii) a corporate minute book with resolutions establishing Canadian-nexus treasury control; (iv) a notarized Source of Funds and Source of Wealth declaration for each UBO; (v) the group's organizational chart identifying the ULC's operational role in UI/UX design delivery.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-volume, low-value outgoing electronic fund transfers to multiple overseas subcontractor designers may resemble layering or cross-border disbursement without documented delivered services.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Maintain and present: (i) sub-contractor agreements with scope, deliverables, and fixed-fee schedules; (ii) approved invoice register and milestone completion certificates; (iii) Stripe Billing export showing matching subscription inflow; (iv) a Treasury Policy Memorandum authorizing the disbursement calendar and FX conversion methodology; (v) the bank's required purpose codes (e.g., ISO 20215 Category Purpose 'SUPP' or 'S3010' for design services) on each MT103.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: The subscription business may serve customers in US and EU jurisdictions, creating sanctions and third-party payment (Stripe) exposure that banks screen against OFAC/UN/EU lists.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide: (i) a client KYC whitelist with legal entity names and countries; (ii) the ULC's written sanctions-screening procedure covering Stripe sub-merchants; (iii) PCI-DSS attestation of compliance for the billing environment; (iv) the bank's 'Commercial Activity Declaration' completed and signed; (v) an undertaking to notify the bank of any new jurisdiction of customer residence prior to onboarding.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Compliant routing for capital contributions from the US parent or other group entities to the Alberta ULC: (i) execute a corporate resolution of both entities authorizing the contribution (share capital or shareholder loan) and stating account numbers and referencing the ULC's bank and SWIFT BIC; (ii) wire via SWIFT MT103 from the remitting bank (or Fedwire via the US bank's Canadian correspondent) to the ULC's CAD or USD operational account; (iii) include a beneficiary-name match to the registered ULC legal name exactly and use Remittance Information field (72) with clear narrative: 'Capital Contribution – Share Issuance' or 'Shareholder Loan Advance'; (iv) for USD wires, route through the Canadian bank's New York clearing correspondent (e.g., RBC via RBC Bank (Georgia) N.A. or BMO via BMO Harris) and use the Canadian bank's USD ABA/SWIFT BIC; (v) for CAD wires, clear in real-time through Lynx (Bank of Canada's RTGS system) using the account-holding bank's institution number and transit number; (vi) the receiving Canadian bank will report the EFT to FINTRAC if the amount is C$10,000 or greater, which is automatic and not a restriction; (vii) the ULC must retain the SWIFT confirmation, board resolution, and share-register entry to evidence the capital receipt for CRA and Part XIII withholding audit (share capital and arm's-length loans are free of withholding); (viii) if the contribution is in kind (e.g., intellectual property), use a non-wire valuation report and registry transfer, not a clearing rail. The ULC must not use a personal consumer wire or digital currency transfer for capital injection; only bank-to-bank MT103 or Fedwire is acceptable.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Primary clearing rails for trade settlements: (i) SWIFT MT103 for all cross-border payments to subcontract UI/UX designers (EUR/USD/CAD) with applicable purpose codes (ICC Trade Purpose or BPM6 services code S3010; SWIFT category purpose 'SUPP' or 'INTC'); (ii) Lynx (Bank of Canada RTGS) for same-day domestic CAD disbursements above C$25,000; (iii) Automated Clearing Settlement System (ACSS) for Canadian payroll and vendor payments under C$25,000; (iv) Interac e-Transfer or Visa Debit for small incidental expenses (design-asset purchases, software subscriptions); (v) Commercial Letter of Credit (UCP600) is permissible, but not operationally efficient, for white-label development procurement where a third-party escrow condition is required; a Standby L/C (ISP98) may be issued to the US parent as a performance guarantee for enterprise clients; (vi) Stripe Billing remains the collection rail for client subscriptions, with settlement into the ULC operational account via the Canadian bank's acquiring settlement; (vii) for USD supplier payments, the ULC may pre-fund a USD account and execute internal sweep conversions only with a documented bank FX rate; direct CAD-to-USD MT103s will be converted at the bank's spot rate automatically unless an FX forward is pre-booked; (viii) each MT103 must include the invoice number, contract reference, and full beneficiary bank details (BIC/IBAN or ABA) to avoid OFAC name-match delays; (ix) no Commercial LC is required for design services, but if used, confirm with a Canadian bank and include a 5-business-day availability and documents clause; (x) all outbound wires must be approved by a second authorized signatory per the ULC's dual-control treasury policy.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable OTC FX forward contracts (CAD/USD, CAD/EUR) with a Tier-1 Schedule I Canadian bank under an ISDA Master Agreement or FX Master Agreement; tenors up to 24 months, collateral-free for lines below C$5 million.
FX options (European-style plain-vanilla) for USD call/CAD put and USD put/CAD call, purchased from the primary clearing bank; premiums expensed through the operational account.
Cross-currency swaps (CAD/USD, CAD/EUR) for matched funding of a US-parent shareholder loan; requires ISDA CSA collateralization if not embedded in the loan agreement.
Exchange-traded CAD/USD futures on the Montréal Exchange (MX) or CME for micro-hedging of short-dated subscription receipts; settled through a licensed futures commission merchant.

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) are NOT permissible for CAD (freely convertible); however, if the ULC invoices a restricted-currency client (e.g., CNY, INR, KRW) and cannot access the onshore deliverable market, an offshore CNY or INR NDF may be executed through the Canadian bank's Hong Kong or London booking desk, provided the Canadian entity does not maintain a cross-border derivative book and the NDF is cleared and confirmed on standard ISDA documentation.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after the anniversary of incorporation
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty of CAD 200; failure to file for two consecutive years may result in administrative strike-off or dissolution by the Alberta Registrar.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No statutory compulsory audit thresholds apply to a private Alberta ULC. An independent auditor must be appointed if shareholder(s) holding at least 5% of voting shares make a written request, or if required by lender or investor agreements. Offering (public) corporations are always subject to mandatory audit.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Private enterprises may choose ASPE (Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises) or IFRS as permitted under CPA Canada Handbook. IFRS is mandatory for public companies.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Alberta has not implemented a separate annual UBO confirmation filing. However, the corporation must update its register of members within 15 days of any share transfer or change in control, and ensure member and directorship records remain current. Failure to maintain registers is an offence under the Alberta Business Corporations Act.

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: $5,000 - $20,000 USD per annum for a typical small private company audit

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 23.0% combined headline rate (15% federal Part I general corporate rate after federal abatement and general rate reduction; 8% Alberta general corporate rate). Alberta ULCs are not eligible for the 11% small business rate when controlled by a non-resident or a corporation.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit available for qualifying UI/UX research and development: 35% refundable credit for CCPCs and 15% non-refundable credit for non-CCPC ULCs on eligible expenditures. Royalty income from software and digital design subscriptions may qualify for the 0% treaty rate on copyright royalties under the Canada-U.S. Treaty. Alberta does not levy capital tax or franchise tax, and offers a 8% general corporate rate with the federal accelerated capital cost allowance (full expensing of eligible digital and computer equipment) available.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (Federal) – CRA EFILE / NETFILE / My Business Account portal, with Alberta provincial tax integrated via the Canada-Alberta single tax administration agreement. Alberta AT1 is submitted as part of the T2 package.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: T2 return must be filed within 6 months after the corporation's fiscal year-end. Estimated income tax instalments under ITA s.157(1) are due quarterly on the last day of each quarter for most corporations; the final balance of Part I tax is due 2 months after year-end (3 months for federal Part I where the small business deduction is claimed, but not applicable for non-CCPC ULC). Alberta corporate tax instalment and balance deadlines mirror the federal schedule.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Cover Page – Box 310 (Legal Name and Business Number)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Registered legal name, Alberta corporate access number, CRA 9-digit Business Number (BN) plus 4-digit program account suffix 'A' for corporate income tax, fiscal year-end date, incorporation jurisdiction, and principal business activity code (NAICS 541430).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Provide the ULC's Canada branch? No, the ULC is a Canadian-resident corporation; identify the U.S. parent and its U.S. Employer Identification Number (EIN) only in Schedule 7 / T106 if the parent is a non-arm's-length non-resident shareholder. If the ULC is disregarded under U.S. check-the-box, it still files a Canadian T2 as a domestic corporation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Gross revenue from design-as-a-service subscription contracts, setup fees, recurring monthly/annual UI-UX design subscriptions, and any associated consulting income. Recognized on an accrual basis; deferred revenue for advance billing must be recorded on the balance sheet schedule.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report revenue from foreign clients (U.S. and other) in the same gross revenue line; no Canadian source grouping needed provided the services are not rendered in Canada for Canadian clients. T2 Schedule 91/93 (Foreign Tax Credit) must be completed if foreign withholding taxes were borne on foreign design-service receipts.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 1 – Line 360 (Federal Part I Tax)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal corporate tax computation: 38% basic rate less 10% provincial abatement less 13% general rate reduction = 15% general rate on taxable income. Line 360 shows federal tax before credits. Deduct SR&ED ITC and foreign tax credits on the applicable schedules.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: These federal fields remain standard for the ULC; no reduced Part I rate applies merely due to non-resident ownership. The ULC must not claim the small business deduction, as the ULC is not a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 5 (Alberta AT1) – Alberta Corporate Income Tax
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Computation of Alberta taxable income allocated to Alberta and 8% provincial corporate income tax. Alberta taxable income equals taxable income for federal purposes adjusted for Alberta's specific marks (no material corporate adjustments for design service entities).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Apply the Alberta allocation formula (labor, revenue, and property factors) if the ULC sells across multiple Canadian provinces; for a wholly Alberta-based remote design team, allocable share will typically be 100%.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Report paid-up capital (PUC), contributed surplus, retained earnings, intercompany loan balance, and dividends declared. The ULC's unlimited liability feature does not alter GAAP equity presentation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Disclose any shareholder loans from the U.S. parent. An intercompany loan bearing interest below arm's length triggers ITA s.247 transfer pricing adjustment and Part XIII interest withholding on the excess deemed benefit.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T106 Information Return for Non-Arm's Length Transactions
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Mandatory return listing all specified transaction amounts with the non-resident U.S. parent or affiliated companies, including management fees, royalties, license fees, R&D cost sharing, intercompany loans, and dividend distributions.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: File T106 when the aggregate fair market value of specified transactions with non-arm's-length non-residents exceeds CAD 1,000,000 in the taxation year. Even below this amount, contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation must be prepared and retained for CRA review.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 7 (Deductions / Dividends) and Form NR4/Part XIII WHT fields
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Capture taxable dividends paid or deemed paid to the U.S. parent and Part XIII non-resident withholding tax liability. Also record any capital dividend election (CDA) if ESDT dividends are paid to reduce PUC or distribute safe income in tax planning.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use the 5% Canada-U.S. Treaty dividend rate only if the U.S. parent owns at least 10% of the ULC's voting stock and Form NR301 has been filed in advance or a verified U.S. IRS Form 6166 certificate of residence is attached to the T2 package. Without valid treaty documentation, the statutory 25% Part XIII rate applies.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late T2 filing penalty: 5% of unpaid Part I tax plus 1% per full month for up to 12 months; 10% plus 2% per month for a second offence. Late or incomplete T106/T1134 filings attract penalties of CAD 2,500 each for separate international information returns; a late Schedule 125 GIFI can attract CAD 100 per day up to CAD 2,500. Interest (daily compounding) is charged on unpaid corporate tax under ITA s.161. Willful failure to file is a criminal offence under ITA s.238, carrying fines of up to CAD 25,000 and imprisonment of up to 12 months.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% under ITA Part XIII on all dividends paid or deemed paid to a non-resident shareholder; reduced to 5% under the Canada-U.S. Tax Treaty (Art. X(2)(a)) when the beneficial owner is a U.S. company owning at least 10% of the ULC's voting shares and the dividends are paid out of active business income.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: 1. Obtain U.S. IRS Form 6166 Certificate of Residency. 2. Submit CRA Form NR301 'Application for a Reduction in the Amount of Non-Resident Tax' before or at the time of the dividend remittance to obtain a reduced Part XIII withholding authorization. 3. Withhold at the 5% treaty rate only after CRA approval is in hand or, in the absence of approval, withhold the full 25%, then file Form NR7-R for refund and remit the difference. 4. File the T2/NR4 summary of dividends and attach the treaty documents for audit trail. 5. Ensure the U.S. parent qualifies as the 'beneficial owner' and passes the limitation-on-benefits provision of the Canada-U.S. Treaty; substantive commercial activity in the ULC and real employees are required to defeat an anti-treaty-shopping challenge.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory Part XIII withholding on royalties: 25%; treaty-reduced to 10% for design and UI-UX copyright/patent royalties, and 0% for software copyright royalties paid to a U.S. resident beneficial owner. Statutory withholding on interest: 25%; treaty-reduced to 0% for arm's length interest paid to a U.S. resident (Canada-U.S. Art. XI, as amended by the 2007 Protocol), except participating/contingent interest which remains taxable at 25%.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: CAD 1,000,000 aggregate fair market value of specified transactions with non-arm's-length non-residents triggers the mandatory T106 information return. There is no statutory CAD threshold for a contemporaneous TP documentation file; all ULCs must prepare a Local File and simplified Master File documenting the design-service intercompany pricing, functional and risk analysis, and benchmark of subscription design services under OECD and CRA Transfer Pricing Memos.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Alberta does not apply UK-style Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) with annual substance tests, but Canadian jurisprudence and tax administration enforce a substance anti-avoidance doctrine: (i) ITA s.245(GARR) invalidates transactions whose primary purpose is tax avoidance and misrepresents economic substance; (ii) the 'beneficial ownership' doctrine under the Canada-U.S. Treaty denies treaty relief where the ULC lacks real Canadian management activity, real employees, and functional office presence; (iii) CRA may re-characterize a ULC holding only a U.S. 10% membership in a U.S. LLC as a sham under the 'step transaction' doctrine. For an ISIC 7410 digital design subscription business, the ULC must maintain actual designers, UI-UX engineers, sales staff, contracts, invoices, bank accounts, and regulatory substance in Alberta; otherwise, CRA can treat the Canadian ULC as an artificial conduit and impute all revenue to the U.S. parent or assess the parent's deemed dividend under s. 84(2).

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion – Willful Intent / Fraudulent Misrepresentation
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberately omitting SaaS/design subscription revenue from the T2, posting fabricated intercompany invoices or margin loans to shift Canadian profits to a U.S. 'escape entity' (LLC), claiming false SR&ED credits on unsubstantiated UI-UX R&D, or back-dating contracts to avoid transfer pricing adjustment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: ITA s. 239(1): fine of 50% to 200% of the tax sought to be evaded; imprisonment up to 5 years on indictment, or up to 2 years on summary conviction; additional civil penalty of 50% of the tax benefit plus full gross-up on reassessment. CRA will disallow all deductions connected to the fraudulent T2 and charge added interest from the original filing due date.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly participate in filing a false or deceptive T2 are jointly and severally liable for the corporation's unpaid tax and penalties under ITA s. 227.1 and may face separate criminal indictment; civil restitution orders and a CRA application to prevent a director from leaving Canada can be obtained when the director's unpaid tax liability exceeds CAD 25,000 and a serious flight risk exists. Conviction on indictment leads to imprisonment of up to 5 years plus lifetime prohibition from serving as director of a Canadian corporation.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company – Absence of Economic Substance / Treaty Shopping
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: The AB ULC has zero employees, no active business, no Alberta office, no design contracts or invoices, and exists purely as a U.S. tax-planning conduit to flow the U.S. parent's future sale gain from an exit without Canadian attribution of business income; while it may artificially create Canadian residence and book foreign design revenue, CRA will reconstruct the ULC's 'periode' under the beneficial ownership doctrine.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: CRA denial of the 5%/0% treaty rates under the limitation-on-benefits and beneficial-ownership principles; reassessment of full Part XIII 25% withholding tax on the dividend stream; application of GAAR under s. 245(2) to re-characterize all shareholder loans and deemed dividends; 100% GAAR penalty under s. 245(4) plus interest and compound penalties; revocation of the corporation's Alberta registration or a compliance order dissolving the ULC.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of the shell ULC are held personally liable for Part XIII withholding tax not remitted from dividends or royalties (s. 227.1); CRA can assess each director personally and seize personal bank accounts. In aggravated cases involving cross-border U.S. tax abuse, a court may issue a travel ban pending extradition or impose personal fines equal to all tax benefits realized by the shareholder chain.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Charging below-arm's-length subscription design service fees to the U.S. parent, recording inflated trademark/royalty payments to the U.S. parent for 'UI-UX brand', failing to prepare a TP benchmark study, failing to file T106 while aggregates exceed CAD 1,000,000, or using the ULC as a cost center with unrealistic profit split.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: ITA s. 247(2) reassessment adjusting income to the arm's-length stage; penalty under s. 247(3) of 10% of the gross transfer-pricing adjustment; the penalty is waived only if the taxpayer has made 'reasonable efforts to determine arm's-length prices'; late T106 filings attract an additional CAD 2,500 per return; interest accrues on the revised tax, and a repeated gross adjustment may trigger criminal prosecution under the Tax Evasion provisions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who sign the T2 while knowing that the TP documentation is incomplete or fraudulent are jointly liable for the 10% TP penalty and the underlying adjusted Part I tax under s. 227.1; in cases of flagrant manipulations, directors face personal criminal liability and a CRA demand for restitution of up to CAD 200,000 plus legal costs.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to register persons with significant control (PSC) on Alberta's corporate registry after the federal Corporate Transparency Act-style register became operative; using a tax haven nominee as shareholder of the AB ULC, concealing the true U.S. parent from the bank when opening a Wise or Stripe payment account, or receiving large, unexplained cross-border funds without a Canadian AML analysis.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Canada's Beneficial Ownership Registry and AML rules impose monetary penalties of up to CAD 500,000 against the corporation; directors can be fined up to CAD 200,000; the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act sets a criminal sanction of up to 10 years imprisonment plus forfeiture of all assets obtained through the concealed structure; banks and payment processors (including Stripe and Wise) report suspicious transactions and can freeze payouts.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are personally liable for civil penalties in the amount of the undeclared funds, and for imprisonment for up to 10 years if the concealment is linked to money laundering as defined under the Criminal Code (s. 462.31); flight-risk directors may be subject to a court-order travel ban pending criminal proceedings; revocation of the ULC's corporate status exposes the entire share capital and personal assets of the directors to creditor claims, given the unlimited liability feature of the ULC.
